issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident, 'Babies' as a salient auditory trigger is hard to connect clinically unless the accident specifically involved infants/crying, which is not supported by the rest of the profile. The other trigger items (intrusive thoughts, nightmare residue) are generic trauma reactivation cues, making this item stand out as trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Make sure never to be alone with another person' suggests avoidance linked to fear of being accused of harming someone or of interpersonal/sexual threat, which is not coherently supported by the accident trauma type, threat items, or appraisals. The rest of the profile is organized around generalized danger/vulnerability, not being alone with another person specifically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after an accident, but here it lacks support from the other selected items. The threat and strategy items focus on physical danger and hypervigilance, while no memory or trigger content suggests shame-based social exposure. In this profile, humiliation is the least coherent appraisal and appears disconnected from the accident-focused formulation.

vignette:
Thao was thirty-two years old, working as a physical therapist in a busy outpatient clinic in Portland, when a driver ran a red light and T-boned his sedan at fifty miles per hour. The impact crushed the driver’s side door into his left hip and thigh, fractured his pelvis in three places, and sent him into a six-week hospital stay that required two surgeries and a month of bed rest. For the first several weeks, he could not bear weight on his left leg, and even after discharge, he walked with a cane for another three months. What stayed with him, though, was not the pain of recovery but the split second before impact—the sound of the other car’s engine, the flash of metal in his peripheral vision, the way his body had been utterly useless. He had always thought of himself as strong, capable, someone who could handle emergencies. Now, whenever he heard a sudden loud noise—a car backfiring, a door slamming, a piece of equipment dropping in the clinic—he felt his chest tighten and his eyes dart to the nearest exit. The noise would send him scanning the room, checking for anything that could be used as a weapon: a pair of scissors left on the counter, a heavy dumbbell on the floor, a fire extinguisher mounted on the wall. He noticed these objects everywhere now, even in places that had never felt dangerous before. The concentration he needed for his work—carefully guiding a patient through a set of hamstring stretches, monitoring their form, adjusting their alignment—became harder to sustain. He would catch himself staring at the door instead of the patient’s knee, his mind pulled away by a sound that had already passed.

The loud noises also brought back a thought that had taken root during his hospital stay: that his body had been permanently damaged. He could feel it when he stood up from a chair and his hip clicked, or when he tried to run and his left leg felt heavy and uncoordinated. He had come to believe that his body was no longer something he could rely on—that it could fail him again at any moment, and that there was no way to know who or what would cause the next harm. This sense of vulnerability bled into his daily life in ways he had not anticipated. At home, after a nightmare woke him—dreams of the crash, always the same, the metal folding, the glass spraying—he would get up and clean the kitchen. He would organize the spice rack by height, then by color, then by frequency of use. It was the only thing that made him feel, even for a few minutes, that he had some control over his surroundings. During the day, he found himself mentally rehearsing worst-case scenarios: what he would do if a patient suddenly became violent, if the fire alarm went off and the building had to be evacuated, if he got into his car and the brakes failed. He knew these rehearsals were excessive, but they also made him feel prepared, and the feeling of being prepared was the only thing that quieted the jumpiness in his chest. His wife had started to notice that he checked the locks three times before bed, and that he flinched when she touched him unexpectedly. She asked if he was okay. He said he was fine.

But he was not fine. The scanning and the rehearsing and the organizing were taking up more and more of his attention, and the more he scanned for threats, the more threats he found. Every loud noise reminded him that his body was unreliable. Every reminder of his body’s unreliability made him scan harder. The cycle tightened over the months, until he found himself avoiding certain streets on his commute, taking a longer route that added fifteen minutes, because that was the route where the accident had happened. He had not told his supervisor about any of this. He was a physical therapist—he was supposed to be the one who helped people trust their bodies again. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in the clinic when a patient dropped a metal water bottle on the tile floor. The sound was sharp and sudden, and Thao dropped the gait belt he was holding, spun around, and found himself staring at the wall, his hands shaking, his heart pounding so hard he thought he might pass out. The patient asked if he was all right. Thao said he needed a glass of water and walked to the break room, where he stood with his palms flat on the counter and tried to breathe. That evening, he searched online for a therapist who specialized in trauma. He was afraid that if he did not do something, the fear would take over completely. He was also afraid that nothing would help.
